rules.ruleDescription: Nouns ending in -ung are almost always feminine (over 99%). They are typically formed from verbs to denote actions or results.
exceptions: der Schwung (not derived with -ung suffix, root words)

rules.ruleDescription: Nouns ending in -heit are always feminine. They derive abstract conditions or states from adjectives.
Nouns ending in -keit are always feminine. Similar to -heit, they create abstract nouns from adjectives ending in -ig, -lich, or -bar.
Nouns ending in -schaft denote collective bodies, institutions, or relationships and are feminine.
Loanwords of Latin origin ending in -tät correspond to English -ty and are feminine.
Diminutive nouns ending in -chen are always neuter, regardless of biological gender.
Diminutive nouns ending in -lein are always neuter.
Nouns of French or Latin origin ending in -ment are almost universally neuter.
exceptions: der Moment (when meaning 'instant'; 'das Moment' means factor)

rules.ruleDescription: Scientific and institutional nouns of Latin origin ending in -um are neuter.
Nouns ending in -ismus denote movements, doctrines, or philosophies and are masculine.
Agent nouns ending in -er denoting male professions, nationalities, or tools are predominantly masculine.

masculine: Days of the week, months, and seasons (der Montag, der Januar, der Sommer)
Points of the compass and winds (der Norden, der Föhn)
Car brand names (der BMW, der Volkswagen, der Mercedes)
Alcoholic drinks, except beer (der Wein, der Wodka; exception: das Bier)
feminine: Cardinal numbers when used as nouns (die Eins, die Million)
Motorcycle and ship names (die Titanic, die BMW R1250)
Names of airplanes (die Boeing 747, die Lufthansa)
neuter: Infinitives used as nouns (das Essen, das Lernen, das Leben)
Letters of the alphabet and musical notes (das A, das B, das hohe C)
Colors used as nouns (das Blau, das Rot, das Grün)
Most metals and chemical elements (das Gold, das Silber, das Eisen; exception: der Stahl)
